extracted.intended_audience: Treasury and IRS officials implementing the Inflation Reduction Act (and other federal rulewriters/OIRA/OMB staff), plus agency staff responsible for environmental justice, distributional analysis, and hydrogen/carbon-accounting guidance
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and recommended criteria for federal agencies (especially Treasury/IRS) to incorporate distributional equity, environmental justice, meaningful public participation, interagency coordination, and rigorous carbon-accounting into notice-and-comment rulemaking and implementation guidance for the Inflation Reduction Act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordinate with other federal agencies with environmental justice expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: Treasury should consult with other federal agencies and interagency working groups on how best to incorporate equity and environmental justice into their rulemaking processes to fulfill Executive Orders and White House guidance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Engage early with agencies that have existing EJ offices (e.g., EPA Office of Environmental Justice and Civil Rights, DOE Office of Economic Impact and Diversity), the White House Environmental Justice Interagency Council, and the White House Environmental Justice Advisory Council to leverage existing expertise rather than starting from scratch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct robust stakeholder outreach, especially in disadvantaged communities
rubrics_metrics.description: Treasury should conduct robust stakeholder outreach throughout the guidance and rulemaking process, especially in disadvantaged communities, because meaningful public engagement provides data for informed decisions and builds public confidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Engage early and continuously with affected communities, state and local regulators, technical experts, labor and environmental groups; use roundtables and community-specific outreach to gather lived-experience knowledge and reduce litigation risk; design processes to enable meaningful—not just token—participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider distributional effects to meet Justice40 and related Executive Orders
rubrics_metrics.description: To the extent possible, Treasury should consider distributional effects as it develops guidance and regulations to implement the IRA in a way that meets the goals of the Justice40 Initiative and Executive Orders directing agencies to consider racial equity and environmental justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gather sufficiently detailed data and monetized estimates of effects; determine whether expected outcomes are distributionally desirable; weigh distributional desirability of options against one another; underpin distributional analysis with robust stakeholder engagement and interagency data-sharing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess regulatory impacts at a granular spatial scale
rubrics_metrics.description: OMB (and agencies) should advise agencies to assess regulatory impacts on a more granular scale (e.g., zip codes, census blocks) when practicable to unveil environmental injustices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use detailed spatial modeling to assess how different small geographies are affected by changes in pollution and other risks; account for baseline exposure levels and existing vulnerabilities; granularity facilitates accurate mortality/morbidity and distributional assessments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disaggregate costs and benefits among demographic subgroups
rubrics_metrics.description: OMB should provide comprehensive guidance to agencies on how to disaggregate their total cost and benefit estimates to illuminate whether any economic or demographic group can be expected to disproportionately bear burdens or receive benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standardize the groups on which analyses should focus (via stakeholder process); provide methodological guidance on disaggregation, and enable comparison/aggregation of distributional impacts across rulemakings and agencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide prescriptive guidance on incorporating distributional analysis into decisionmaking
rubrics_metrics.description: OMB should offer suggestions for how agencies should act on distributional analyses—i.e., how to weigh distributional findings against aggregate benefits/costs in regulatory choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommend qualitative assessments and quantitative tools (inequality metrics, social welfare function weights, weighted cost-benefit analysis); offer approaches for when and how to give distributional impacts decisional weight and when to seek compensatory interagency actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use quantitative tools for evaluating distributional outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should consider quantitative methods—such as inequality metrics, weights based on social welfare functions, or weighted cost-benefit analysis—to evaluate distributional outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OMB could recommend specific metrics or weighting approaches to facilitate consistency; where appropriate, calculate net welfare using weighted cost-benefit analysis to reflect distributional preferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt whole-of-government strategies to mitigate cross-rulemaking disparities
rubrics_metrics.description: Not all regulatory imbalances can be fixed rule-by-rule; OMB should lead interagency strategies to identify and compensate groups disproportionately burdened across the regulatory system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop coordinated, interagency strategies and provide systemwide oversight; use compensatory actions in other agencies or spending programs when changing individual rules is infeasible; publish regular OMB reports on disparate impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design stakeholder engagement processes to capture ‘situated knowledge’
rubrics_metrics.description: Public participation—especially from environmental justice communities—provides unique, lived-experience information about impacts and can identify ambiguities, gaps, and unintended consequences not apparent to formal experts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create engagement formats that enable communities to convey contextual knowledge; ensure participation is meaningful (timely, accessible, responsive) to improve data quality and public confidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordinate early with state and local regulators and technical experts
rubrics_metrics.description: Treasury should engage with federal, state, and local regulators and other technical experts early because IRA tax credits overlap with state policies and other regulations (e.g., siting, permitting) that affect distributional outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early coordination can harness state expertise on distribution of funds, align complementary policies, and reduce the risk of costly litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gather sufficiently detailed data and monetize distributional effects where possible
rubrics_metrics.description: A key aspect of distributional analysis is gathering sufficiently detailed data and monetized estimates of effects to reveal how benefits and costs are distributed across subpopulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use interagency data-sharing and working groups to obtain needed granularity; attach monetized and non-monetized distributional descriptions in decision documents per Circular A-4 guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use marginal emissions rates with spatial and temporal granularity for hydrogen carbon accounting
rubrics_metrics.description: To quantify emissions from grid electricity associated with electrolytic hydrogen, agencies should endorse the use of marginal emissions rates with appropriate spatial and temporal granularity—i.e., focus on the carbon intensity of the power plant that increases generation to match the new load.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Marginal-emissions approaches reflect the actual emissions from additional load, are administrable using available data (PJM, MISO, ISO-NE, WattTime, EIA developments), and better incentivize hydrogen production during periods/places of renewable curtailment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require temporal granularity (hourly or sub-hourly) for marginal emissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Temporal resolution must be sufficiently granular (hourly or sub-hourly) because marginal emissions rates change as frequently as grid dispatch and annual averages misrepresent the emissions impact of additional load.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use hourly/sub-hourly marginal-emissions estimates (real-time or near-real-time) so electrolysis timing can be properly assessed and incentivized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require spatial granularity aligned with grid-balancing-authority footprints
rubrics_metrics.description: Marginal emissions rates vary by geography; agencies should use spatially granular marginal emissions rates that align with balancing-authority footprints (or smaller where available) to reflect actual emissions caused by regional electricity consumption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: GREET’s large regional averages do not align with operational grid boundaries; instead, use balancing-authority-level or finer marginal data to calculate location-specific carbon intensity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Update GREET or adopt a successor model incorporating marginal-emissions approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Because GREET currently uses average grid mixes and annual averages, Treasury should cooperate with DOE to update GREET to a marginal-emissions approach or develop a successor model under the Secretary’s discretion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If GREET is not promptly updated, Treasury should use discretionary authority to adopt a successor modeling approach that incorporates spatial and temporal marginal emissions rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require additionality for RECs and PPAs used to claim emission offsets
rubrics_metrics.description: If electrolyzers use RECs, PPAs, or other instruments to offset grid electricity emissions, the renewable generation associated with those instruments must be additional to the grid (i.e., would not have been produced but for the instrument).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absent additionality, REC or PPA-based offsets merely reshuffle allocation on paper and should not be recognized; require demonstrations/tests of additionality (acknowledging multiple possible tests) before allowing offsets to reduce hydrogen carbon intensity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for avoided emissions from RECs/PPAs using spatially and temporally specific marginal emissions rates
rubrics_metrics.description: Assuming additionality is satisfied, the avoided-emissions value of an REC or PPA depends on when and where the clean generation operated; agencies should calculate displaced emissions using marginal emissions rates for the time and place of generation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: RECs associated with generation that displaced coal/gas at a given time/location have high avoided-emissions value; RECs generated during curtailment (when marginal emissions = 0) should not be credited as offsets for hydrogen produced at other times/places.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish physical PPAs and financial/virtual PPAs in accounting
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical PPAs that deliver clean power to an electrolyzer within a single region and time can produce zero carbon intensity for that power (assuming additionality), whereas financial/virtual PPAs require avoided-emissions accounting using marginal emissions for residual market purchases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If clean generator cannot supply all contracted power, the carbon intensity of purchased wholesale energy is the marginal plant’s emissions at the time/place of generation; account for such residual sourcing accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not allow RECs to offset emissions when the clean generation occurred during curtailment
rubrics_metrics.description: When clean resources are being curtailed, marginal emissions are zero; RECs tied to energy produced during curtailment displace no emissions and therefore should not be used to claim avoided emissions for electrolyzer load elsewhere or at other times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use temporally and spatially granular marginal estimates to determine whether a REC corresponds to genuine avoided emissions; disallow offset claims when generation occurred during curtailment with zero marginal emissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design clear standards and best practices for environmental justice assessment and mitigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should articulate clear policies, standards, and best practices for evaluating environmental justice impacts, including identification of EJ communities, selection of study areas and reference populations, and articulable mitigation measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lack of clear guidelines diminishes accountability and makes it harder for affected parties to anticipate agency actions; agencies can draw lessons from FERC proceedings and public-interest organization recommendations for EJ assessment improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider cumulative impacts across programs and use compensatory actions when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Some disparities become evident only when viewed cumulatively across multiple rulemakings; agencies and OMB should consider systemwide patterns and use compensatory measures when changing an individual rule is not the most effective remedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coordinate across agencies and programs to identify groups disproportionately burdened and apply regulatory or spending authorities elsewhere to mitigate inequities; regular OMB reporting can facilitate this process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Underpin distributional analysis with robust stakeholder engagement and data collection
rubrics_metrics.description: Distributional analysis should be supported by stakeholder engagement to obtain accurate data, community concerns, and locally relevant information that improves the granularity and credibility of analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use community input to identify relevant subpopulations and vulnerabilities, supplement administrative and modeled data, and ensure that distributional assessments reflect lived experience and public priorities.
